entities.summary:
J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur, naturalized in New York as John Hector St. John, was a French-American writer, diplomat, and farmer. Born on January 31, 1735, in Caen, France, de Crèvecœur was educated at the École Militaire in Paris and later served as a diplomat in France and the United States. He was a key figure in the development of American literature, and his influential work, 'Letters from an American Farmer,' published in 1787, shaped the national identity of the United States. De Crèvecœur's writing often explored the themes of colonialism, frontier life, and the American Revolution. He died on November 12, 1813, in New York City.

De Crèvecœur's significance can be seen in his role as a mediator between the French and American cultures, and his work as a diplomat helped shape the United States' early foreign policy. His writing also had a lasting impact on American literature, influencing writers such as Thomas Jefferson and James Madison. The American Revolution's impact on the world is a testament to de Crèvecœur's legacy.

The legacy of J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur can be seen in the development of American literature and the nation's early foreign policy. His work continues to be studied by historians and scholars today, offering valuable insights into the colonial era and the American Revolution.

In 2018, de Crèvecœur was posthumously inducted into the French Literary and Philosophical Society, recognizing his contributions to French-American literature and culture.

De Crèvecœur's impact on American literature and culture is undeniable. His writing continues to inspire scholars and writers today, offering a unique perspective on the colonial era and the American Revolution.

De Crèvecœur's legacy extends beyond literature, with his diplomatic work shaping the United States' early foreign policy. His influence can be seen in the development of the country's national identity and its relationships with other nations.
